articles.title: Biosynthetic allene and alkyne formation by enzymatic prenyl demethylation
articles.abstract: Abstract Allenes and alkynes are versatile functional groups in chemical biology and drug discovery. However, how nature biosynthetically installs them in natural products, especially allenes, remains poorly understood. Here we uncovered that allenes and alkynes can be formed enzymatically through oxidative C( sp 2 )-demethylation of the common five-carbon prenyl group. Two fungal cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, PpnB and NseB, from the penipratynolene and sinuxylamide biosynthetic pathways, respectively, were shown to catalyze oxidative removal of a C( sp 2 )-methyl group in O -prenyl l -tyrosine to afford O -homoallenyl l -tyrosine and O -but-2-ynyl l -tyrosine, respectively. Combining density functional theory calculations and biochemical assays with isotopically labeled substrates, a mechanism involving selective C–C bond cleavage followed by product-determining hydrogen atom abstraction is presented. An additional P450 enzyme from the penipratynolene pathway, PpnD, acts as an oxidative isomerase that converts the four-carbon terminal allene into a terminal alkyne. This sophisticated enzymatic editing strategy to install allene and alkyne expands the catalytic repertoire of P450 enzymes.

articles.title: Nitrene generation and transfer for unnatural biosynthesis in living cells
articles.abstract: Abstract Synthetic biology has enabled the production of natural and unnatural products from inexpensive sustainable feedstocks. Yet, the scope of available products has been limited largely to compounds accessible from nature’s chemical reactions. Evolved enzymes can catalyse reactions of unnatural substrates or reactions not found in nature but often require the addition of synthetic reagents to purified enzymes or to resting cells containing those enzymes. Here we show that chemical reactions of metabolic intermediates produced intracellularly in living cells can include intermolecular nitrene transfers. The biosynthesis of N -acetoxyanilines, in combination with the generation and transfer of N -aryl nitrene intermediates from them catalysed by a cytochrome P450, generates amino alcohols, diamines, diarylamines and aminoalkyl arenes from simple carbon feedstocks. These products—common substructures of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals—are challenging to synthesize by standard organic chemistry and were produced from inexpensive, renewable feedstocks. Evolution of the enzymes in this pathway showed that titres can be increased by engineering and that the products can be synthesized with high enantioselectivity.
articles.authors: Isaac Donnell · Andrew Quest · Jeremy Tang

articles.title: Revised Biosynthetic Pathway of Alnumycin Involves a Complex Interplay of Redox Reactions, Stereoisomerization, and an Atypical DUF6081 Isomerase
articles.abstract: Abstract Alnumycin A is an antimicrobial natural product distinguished by an unusual 1,3-dioxane moiety attached to an aromatic polyketide core. While previous studies had established that d-ribose serves as the precursor to the 1,3-dioxane and its attachment to the aromatic ring system is catalyzed by a C-glycoside synthase, less is known about its subsequent transformation. Aln6 is a member of the domain of unknown function (DUF) 6081 protein family and was previously annotated as a cofactor-free oxidase. Herein, Aln6 is shown to catalyze a redox-neutral isomerization that converts the ribose moiety to a fused furan-dioxolane via an unprecedented rearrangement mechanism. Aln4 subsequently catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reductive ring-opening of the furan, setting the stage for nonenzymatic rearrangement of the dioxolane that produces the 1,3-dioxane structure and explains the stereochemical diversity of alnumycin A observed in vivo. Together, these findings not only revise the established view of the late-stage biosynthesis of alnumycin A but also redefine the chemistry of Aln6, expanding the catalytic repertoire of the DUF6081 family beyond canonical oxidative reactions.

articles.title: MucD regulates alginate biosynthesis through the proteolytic control of AlgX and AlgK in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
articles.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic human pathogen capable of infecting a wide range of tissues and organs. Its persistence during chronic infection is strongly associated with biofilm formation, which depends on extracellular polysaccharides such as alginate. The HtrA-like periplasmic serine protease MucD is a key regulator of bacterial virulence, stress response, and alginate production, yet its molecular mechanism has remained largely unclear. Here, we discovered the alginate acetylation and export proteins AlgX and AlgK as MucD substrates, and characterized their degradation by mass spectrometry and bioinformatic analysis. We further determined the cryo-EM structure of MucD bound to an AlgK-derived substrate peptide, offering atomic insights into MucD oligomerization assembly, substrate recognition, and specificity. Together with structure-guided mutagenesis and biochemical assays, our results revealed that MucD proteolytic activity is governed by an equilibrium between a resting 12-mer and an active trimer. Crucially, we demonstrate that MucD represses alginate biosynthesis post-translationally, in addition to its previously implicated role in transcriptional regulation. These findings define a distinct activation mechanism and regulatory function for MucD and provide new insight into bacterial HtrA-like serine proteases.
articles.authors: Yujun Jiang · Xin-Fu Yan · Rya Ero

articles.title: De Novo Synthesis of a Highly Strained and Twisted Imide‐Bridged Bicyclic Scaffold
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Embedding functional motifs into bridged scaffolds is a powerful strategy for molecular recognition and drug design, yet imide‐bridged medium‐ring systems have remained synthetically inaccessible. Here, we report an expedient de novo synthesis of imidebridged bicyclo[4.3.1]decane scaffolds, featuring a highly strained anti ‐Bredt olefin and a twisted seven‐membered imide ring, with excellent diastereoselectivity (>20:1 dr). The one‐pot, palladium‐catalyzed sequential reaction of isocyanides with allenyl butenoates proceeds with complete atom economy and high bond‐forming efficiency. Mechanistic studies reveal that efficient leaving‐group recapture and a highly reactive inverse‐electron‐demand type II intramolecular Diels–Alder (IMDA) reaction are both critical to this transformation. Notably, these unprecedented products display promising antiproliferative activity against a panel of cancer cell lines, highlighting their potential for antitumor drug discovery.
